papers.title: Just Ask Jev: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions as a Zero-Shot Detector of AI Alignment Failures
papers.description: Detectors of alignment failures screen deployed language models and score alignment benchmarks. Most are generative judges that spend a decoding pass on every criterion, and classifiers that read token probabilities, such as Llama Guard, still score one fixed label per call. Jev, a model trained with reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions (RLCD), answers many typed questions about one input with calibrated probabilities in a single call. Whether it detects alignment failures has not been measured. We present RLCDAlignBench, which benchmarks Jev on ten alignment failures: sycophancy, jailbreaks, deception, prompt injection, hallucination, privacy violation, social bias, reward hacking, concealing uncertainty, and power seeking. Many of these failures are relational, defined against a reference, such as the user's belief or an injected instruction, that the response alone does not reveal. Our key idea is therefore to vary what Jev is asked separately from what it sees: the question's wording and answer type on one side, the fields of the input on the other. A single generic question reaches a median AUROC of 0.886 zero-shot and beats supervised baselines on most benchmarks. Question wording matters little, while context matters more, mostly through fields that encode the label. Jev matches the reference scorer's agreement with human labels, surfaces label defects in existing benchmarks, and costs 63x less than LLM-judge scorers. papers.title: Jev in the Wild: A Data-Driven Analysis of the Jev Model's Functionality, Applications and Ecosystem
papers.description: Jev is a fast, low-cost decision model that answers natural-language questions with choices, binary judgments, and scores. As its public ecosystem grows rapidly, it remains unclear how Jev is used across applications and how public attention relates to project distribution. To answer these questions, we conduct a large-scale, data-driven analysis of 2,170 publicly available Jev projects collected from GitHub as of September 22, 2026. We find rapid early growth in Jev's public ecosystem, with both new projects and integration into existing repositories. Across diverse domains, projects use Jev for multiple decision purposes and combine its interfaces. Attribute judgment and scoring are widely used, while the use of action selection, content filtering, and model and tool selection varies across domains. These patterns suggest that Jev serves as a reusable decision component whose functionality varies with the surrounding workflow. Meanwhile, public attention is concentrated in routing and interface agents and does not track project counts. Our findings provide a quantitative view of Jev's emerging ecosystem and inform the design and evaluation of general-purpose decision models across diverse application contexts.

papers.title: Decision Without Generation: Benchmarking a Calibrated Non-Generative Decision Model Against LLM Judges on Moderation, Hallucination, NLI and Prompt-Injection Tasks
papers.description: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as judges for content moderation, hallucination detection and prompt-injection filtering, although they are slow, expensive and poorly calibrated when asked to verbalise probabilities. A quantisation control shows the ranking advantage is not an artefact of the LLMs' coarser verbalised probabilities. We report a negative result - no cheap-tier cascade on Jev's uncertain band significantly improves on Jev alone - and two self-caught evaluation artefacts. papers.title: CROW: Classifier-Routed Organization of LLM Wikis
papers.description: LLM wikis have been proposed as an alternative to classical retrieval-augmented generation ( RAG ): a large language model ( LLM ) incrementally organizes knowledge into a directory of notes that can be inspected directly and grows with little manual upkeep, at the price of LLM calls whose cost grows with the knowledge base. Many of these calls are spent on decisions rather than on writing: where a new source belongs, which notes it relates to, which notes answer a question. We introduce CROW ( Classifier-Routed Organization of LLM Wikis ), a decision layer for LLM wikis that delegates these routing and consolidation decisions to a general-purpose typed classifier, such as the recently released Jev, and reserves generative calls for the steps that require writing text. In CROW, ingestion relies on a short sequence of classifier calls and invokes an LLM only to summarize the incoming source, to name new folders and, when an existing note must be updated, to rewrite it, while retrieval uses the classifier to select the relevant notes and leaves to the LLM only the final answer. CROW does not replace the compilation of entity, concept and synthesis pages that gives LLM wikis much of their value. We specify how each decision maps onto classifier primitives, position the design with respect to memory systems for LLM agents, model routing and candidate-then-verify pipelines , and discuss the effects on cost and latency that we expect but have not yet measured, together with the main limitations.

Ingestion uses short sequences of classifier calls to organize sources, invoking the LLM only to summarize content, name folders, or rewrite existing notes. Retrieval similarly employs classifiers to select relevant notes, leaving final answer generation to the LLM.

papers.title: Context-Conditioned Option Selection: A Black-Box Investigation of Jev and the Evolution of a Similarity-Based Decision Model
papers.description: Specialised AI decision models select actions or answers from predefined alternatives given a context and a question. This paper examines whether the observed selection behaviour of Jev can be ap- proximated by context–question–option compatibility scoring followed by probability allocation, rather than treating its outputs as independent verification of correctness. A sequence of exploratory black-box experiments evaluates constraints, missing factual context, fictional facts, invalid choice sets, multiple correct answers, contextual ordering and partial identity matches. When two or three machines were equally eligible, Jev repeatedly assigned dominant probability to the first eligible entity introduced in the context; reversing contextual order reversed that preference, while changing the answer-option or- der had little effect in the recorded comparison. These findings led to a series of explicitly specified algorithms: initial cosine similarity, candidate-specific question rewriting, joint normalisation, neutral context enrichment, lexical and cross-encoder scoring, and sequential probability assignment. ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol in the present authoring session) was used as a retrospective LLM proxy to assess candi- date evidence; the precise model identifier of earlier proxy-scoring turns was not logged. Its scores were illustrative assessments, not measured pretrained cross-encoder outputs or directly extracted hidden em- bedding vectors. The proxy-plus-allocation pipeline reproduces several qualitative Jev selection patterns. We distinguish black-box evidence from proposed mechanisms and specify a reproducible validation pro- tocol. The study does not establish Jev’s internal architecture, a validated accuracy improvement, or a measured runtime advantage. A consolidated per-experiment table distinguishes Jev’s reported choices, the alternative model’s retrospective proxy selections, and objective eligibility.

What is it?
This study investigates the decision-making patterns of an AI system named Jev through black-box experimentation. It tests whether Jev’s outputs can be approximated by scoring context-question-option compatibility and allocating probabilities, rather than treating its choices as independent verifications of correctness.

What the paper actually contributes.
The authors propose a reproducible pipeline using initial cosine similarity, candidate-specific question rewriting, joint normalization, neutral context enrichment, lexical scoring, and cross-encoder scoring. They provide a consolidated table comparing Jev’s choices against a retrospective LLM proxy (ChatGPT) and objective eligibility criteria, distinguishing observed evidence from proposed mechanisms.

Problem solved
Specialized AI models often select actions from predefined alternatives based on context. This research addresses the gap in understanding whether such selections stem from genuine reasoning or simpler compatibility heuristics, specifically examining how missing facts, fictional data, and ordering affect outcomes.

How does it work?
The method employs a proxy-plus-allocation pipeline. It evaluates constraints like invalid choice sets and partial identity matches. The approach uses ChatGPT as a retrospective proxy to assess candidate evidence, though these scores are illustrative assessments rather than measured pretrained cross-encoder outputs or extracted hidden embedding vectors.

Who should use it?
AI researchers and engineers interested in the interpretability of black-box decision models. The work is particularly relevant for those studying similarity-based decision architectures and the impact of contextual ordering on model selection behavior.

Why is it useful?
It clarifies that Jev repeatedly assigns dominant probability to the first eligible entity introduced in the context. Reversing contextual order reverses this preference, while changing answer-option order has little effect. This helps distinguish between complex reasoning and simple positional biases in AI selection.

Key capabilities
The study analyzes contextual ordering, partial identity matches, and multiple correct answers. It utilizes a sequence of exploratory experiments to evaluate constraints and missing factual context, providing a protocol for validating similarity-based decision models.

Maturity/status

papers.title: When Does Selection Replace Extraction? A Pre-Registered Test of Agent Memory with a Typed Decision Model
papers.description: Does conversational memory need LLM-extracted facts, or is selecting the right raw turns enough? Published results disagree. Extraction-based systems report gains from distilled facts. Recent studies find raw history with good ranking does as well, but disagree about whether ranking matters. We ran a pre-registered study on held-out LoCoMo conversations and LongMemEval. At a tight budget on LoCoMo, raw turns selected by a single call to Jev, a typed decision model, are non-inferior to an LLM-extraction memory (one-sided 95% bound −3.0 points against a −5-point margin). Blind human grading narrows the margin but does not change the result. Raw turns cost 3,061× less to write, and the result holds with a second answer model. Within this study, reranking's gain shrinks as the budget grows. It adds 17.4 points on LoCoMo and 9.1 on LongMemEval when three of 30 candidates are kept. At generous budgets it adds 1.5 and 1.1, and extraction systems are more accurate. This suggests why published results disagree. At matched context, Jev selects as accurately as an LLM reranker (non-inferiority bound −2.0) at a third of the latency, and more accurately than a multi-call graph traversal. Reranking lowers correct abstention. Plans, code and graded answers are released. papers.readme:
What is it?
This pre-registered study tests whether selecting raw conversation turns outperforms LLM-based fact extraction for agent memory. The authors compare a typed decision model called Jev against extraction-based systems on held-out LoCoMo conversations and LongMemEval datasets.

Problem solved
Published results on conversational memory are inconsistent. Extraction systems claim gains from distilled facts, while recent studies suggest raw history with ranking performs equally well. This work clarifies why results disagree by analyzing budget constraints and ranking utility.

How does it work?
The team uses Jev, a single-call typed decision model, to select relevant raw turns. They compare this against LLM extraction and reranking methods. The approach avoids distilling facts, relying instead on precise selection of original context segments to maintain fidelity.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers building conversational agents. It is particularly relevant for teams optimizing memory costs and latency in long-context applications.

Why is it useful?
Selected raw turns cost 3,061 times less to write than extracted facts. At tight budgets, Jev is non-inferior to extraction, with a one-sided 95% bound of negative 3.0 points against a negative five-point margin. Reranking benefits shrink as budgets increase, explaining conflicting literature.

Key capabilities
The study utilizes the LoCoMo and LongMemEval datasets. It releases code, plans, and graded answers. Jev matches LLM reranker accuracy at a third of the latency, outperforming multi-call graph traversal. It also lowers incorrect abstention rates.

Performance
Reranking adds 17.4 points on LoCoMo and 9.1 on LongMemEval when keeping three of 30 candidates. At generous budgets, gains drop to 1.5 and 1.1 points respectively. Jev selects as accurately as LLM rerankers with a non-inferiority bound of negative 2.0.

Maturity/status
The work is a preprint published on Zenodo. The study is pre-registered, with plans and amendments publicly available. Code is hosted on GitHub under the Engram repository.

papers.title: Introducing Consort: A Spec-First Agent Framework for Enforced, Test-Driven Development on Live Database Branches
papers.description: When an agent writes code, the development framework becomes the control system for a non-deterministic worker. Spec-first, agent-driven frameworks have gained rapid traction since 2025; the installable ones, GitHub Spec Kit, obra/superpowers, BMAD, and GSD, and our own, all capture intent through a specification or durable planning artifacts. Since they agree on capturing intent up front, what separates them is how each enforces the engineering discipline that keeps agent-written code clean, correct, and maintainable. Every framework enforces that discipline somehow; they differ in how. We characterize three modes: enforcement by persuasion (prompt discipline the model may ignore), by front-loaded structure (strong specs, then a trusted build), and through controls the agent cannot edit (a deterministic orchestrator, human-approved gates, immutable tests, and a green result that must pass against a live, branched database). We introduce Consort, a spec-first, test-driven agent framework built on the third, enforcing that discipline through controls the agent runs inside but cannot bypass, in which a deterministic orchestrator drives separate role agents through a spec-first design lane and a test-driven build lane on a live database branch. We argue that enforcing the tests and gates in code keeps agent-written code honest and verifiable, while its specialized roles, like the human roles before them, are what make it maintainable, claims we frame as a pre-registered, testable hypothesis.
papers.readme:
What is it?
Consort is a spec-first, test-driven agent framework designed for enforced development on live database branches. It addresses the variability in how existing frameworks maintain engineering discipline for non-deterministic AI workers.

Problem solved
Current spec-first frameworks like GitHub Spec Kit or BMAD rely on prompt discipline or front-loaded structures that agents can sometimes bypass. This paper identifies a gap in enforcing immutable constraints, arguing that persuasion or simple structure is insufficient for ensuring code remains clean, correct, and verifiable over time.

How does it work?
Consort operates through a deterministic orchestrator that drives separate role agents through distinct lanes. It utilizes a spec-first design lane followed by a test-driven build lane. Crucially, it enforces discipline through controls the agent cannot edit, including human-approved gates, immutable tests, and a live, branched database environment. The agent runs inside this system but cannot bypass the enforcement mechanisms.

Who should use it?
This framework targets AI engineers, researchers, and technical product readers interested in robust, test-driven development workflows for AI agents. It is particularly relevant for teams requiring strict engineering standards in automated code generation.

Why is useful?
It keeps agent-written code honest and verifiable by separating roles and enforcing immutable tests. This approach mirrors human engineering roles, improving maintainability. The authors frame this as a pre-registered, testable hypothesis regarding the efficacy of enforced controls.

Key capabilities
The system features a deterministic orchestrator, specialized role agents, and integration with live database branches. It supports immutable testing and human-approved gates to ensure compliance.

huggingface.readme:
What is it?
TeleOCR is a lightweight 1.2B parameter vision-language model designed for comprehensive document parsing. It unifies the handling of both digital and camera-captured documents within a single framework.

Problem solved
Existing solutions typically target either clean digital scans or distorted camera photos, forcing users to switch models. TeleOCR addresses this fragmentation by providing robust parsing across both scenarios without requiring separate preprocessing steps like image dewarping.

How does it work?
The architecture employs geometry-aware document modeling and Content-Structure Decoupled Learning for tables and formulas. It utilizes Multi-node Consensus Voting for pseudo-label generation and Curvature-Guided Douglas-Peucker Sampling. The model undergoes a progressive four-stage training pipeline to optimize performance on complex layouts.

Who should use it?
AI engineers, researchers, and technical product developers building document intelligence pipelines. It is particularly suitable for teams needing a single, efficient model to handle mixed input sources in production environments.

Why is it useful?
TeleOCR offers state-of-the-art accuracy while maintaining a small footprint, making it practical for deployment. It eliminates the need for dedicated rectification models by parsing distorted documents directly, streamlining the engineering workflow.

Key capabilities
The model supports text, table, formula, code, and layout extraction. It outputs tables in OTSL format for conversion to HTML and formulas in LaTeX. It handles complex geometric deformations and scientific figures without external preprocessing.

Performance
TeleOCR achieves 96.87 overall accuracy on OmniDocBench v1.6, outperforming larger models like Qwen3-VL-235B. It ranks first in the Dr.DocBench Challenge and ICDAR2026 Sci-ImageMiner competition, demonstrating superior text edit and table parsing metrics.

Maturity/status
The project is an open-source research release under the Apache-2.0 license. Community contributions include GGUF conversion for llama.cpp support, indicating active development and practical utility.
